items.note: Author suggests Khan family's branch was deprived of Rajput Parmar caste identity; descendants of the Sot state may hold memories of lost rule. Community identity of the Parmar descendants.
items.gloss: From Khan Sahib's side we would learn when his ties with Madhya Pradesh broke and what circumstances deprived his branch of the Rajput Parmars' caste identity. The descendants of the Sot state surely hold the threads showing what their ancestors saw over past centuries after being deprived of the throne.

items.note: Author asks whether the temple is only carved stone for governments to look after, or something ordinary people share; frames Udaypur as meaningful to residents (community stewardship).
items.gloss: Is it merely a temple of carved stones, of which India is full, which has survived by luck and for which we can now do nothing, so that only governments must act? Are these monuments with which ordinary people have nothing to do? I think Udaypur is a meaningful purpose for us. For me every such heritage around me is a big question and also an answer.

items.note: Argues preserving the monument is the duty of every citizen of the region, not only Udaypur's panchayat residents; inscriptions as documents of the link with ancestors.
items.gloss: Udaypur is a symbol of India's great cultural identity; if it has survived by luck, preserving this priceless heritage in its original form is nobody else's task. It does not belong only to the residents of Udaypur's panchayat; it belongs to every citizen of the area. Udaypur is a creation of our creative ancestors that still reminds us of our bond with them. The countless inscriptions are documents engraved on the stones of that bond.

items.note: Author's characterisation: the temple as a poem in stone to Shiva, said to have taken three years with thousands of craftsmen from afar (author's assertion; compare other construction-duration statements).
items.gloss: Udaypur is a poem written on stones that the Paramara kings sang in praise of their worshipped Lord Shiva. Composing this praise took three years, and thousands of craftsmen came from who knows where and displayed their art at its best.

claim.value: construction said to take three years (author's statement)

items.note: Large structures taken as evidence of economic prosperity; Udayaditya built the Udayeshvara temple and the general community also contributed many works, which only a financially sound society could do.
items.gloss: Udaypur is also proof of India's rich economic heritage, since such huge creations cannot be the mark of a poor country. If King Udayaditya had the Udayeshvara temple built, the common people of Udaypur also contributed many works here, and only an economically strong society could do that.

items.note: Author reflects on Udaypur's survival through dark periods and 'severe blows of the medieval period', and asks what happened to the Vijay temple at Vidisha.
items.gloss: Udaypur means also listening to the troubles India underwent in a long dark period. This settlement, which looks desolate today, saw the best of lights and was not untouched by countless darknesses. It is a throbbing proof of India's indomitable will. It must have been a land of heroes who faced enemies for centuries, otherwise Udaypur could not have survived the terrible blows of the medieval period. What happened to the Vijay temple at Vidisha?

items.note: Author says revival is not mere polishing to attract outsiders; spread of tourism is a material initiative that should happen without delay, but will be superficial unless Udaypur's call touches the soul.
items.gloss: Udaypur's revival is not merely polishing an ancient temple or settlement and attracting others with the show. Spreading tourism is a physical initiative that should happen without delay. If Udaypur's call cannot touch our soul, these efforts will also be superficial.

items.note: Appeal to historians and archaeologists to visit; mounds need clearing and ruins need excavation.
items.gloss: Udaypur is urging historians and archaeologists to leave books and files, come once and look carefully at every corner. Many new stories lie buried in its womb. Countless pages are fluttering. Cleaning of the mounds is necessary. Excavation of the ruins is necessary.

items.note: Udaypur is said to look for a person like Alexander Cunningham, curious and willing to hear the past's voice and share it.
items.gloss: Udaypur is looking for a good person like Alexander Cunningham, whether engineer or army officer, doctor or teacher, who is full of curiosity and, going beyond his claims, himself hears the voice of the past and makes others hear it too.

items.note: Vision of Udaypur as an invitation to students, writers and poets; stories of dynasties as material for fiction, drama and songs.
items.gloss: Udaypur's lanes await students of schools and colleges daring to peer into the tunnels of India's past. There is much more factual to say than grandmothers' tales. These stories hold the tales of many dynasties of kings. Udaypur is a fertile field for imaginative writers, novelists and poets. There are many threads for novels, plays, stories and songs. Udaypur is eager that someone take these threads and tell how far back his imagination carried him.

items.note: Six-line inscription on a stone at the right of the temple's doorway, recording Vaisakh sudi 7 VS 1137, given as 30 March 1080.
items.gloss: It was written on a stone in six lines. It was written to the right of the door of the temple's (side). It records Vaisakh sudi 7 Vikram Samvat 1137. By the English calendar this date is 30 March 1080.

items.note: Presented as the most important of about a dozen inscriptions found at Udaypur because it is the oldest, 1080, from Udayaditya's time.
items.gloss: Among the dozen inscriptions found in Udaypur it is the most important because it is of 1080. The oldest. From the time of Udayaditya.

items.note: Names the author of the record as Pandit Mahipal, son of Pandit Shringvas, describing the temple's flag-hoisting ceremony.
items.gloss: He is Pandit Mahipal, the illustrious son of Pandit Shringvas, who is telling about the flag-hoisting ceremony at the temple.

items.note: Author imagines the town's former splendour; the collapsing ruins of the royal palace are called the finest witness of that glorious time.
items.gloss: One can only guess what days today's Udaypur, lost in narrow lanes and in poor condition, saw then. The crumbling ruins of the royal palace are the most splendid witness of that glorious time.

items.note: States the temple took more than twenty years to be completed.
items.gloss: This temple, completed over more than twenty years, must have been a topic of talk far and wide even while under construction.

claim.value: built over more than twenty years

items.note: Author's assessment that independent India's governments failed to know or document such heritage; the heritage and archaeology departments should have been activated on 15 August 1947 and every inscription read.
items.gloss: It is the fault of independent India's governments that we do not know even this superficially. India's history, culture and archaeology department should have been activated in top gear on 15 August 1947, and with the help of experts worldwide the saving of every ruined heritage should have begun. Every inscription was to be read.

items.note: INTACH is stated to have traced more than a hundred inscriptions at Udaypur, unknown to residents of Udaypur and Vidisha.
items.gloss: In Udaypur itself INTACH has traced more than a hundred inscriptions. But neither the people of Udaypur know, nor the people of Vidisha.

items.note: Santosh Kumar Verma's account of the oldest inscription: VS 1137 Vaisakh sudi 7, no weekday given, mention of solar transit and karana unnamed; computed as Monday 30 March 1080 CE.
items.gloss: According to young historian Santosh Kumar Verma this inscription is of Vikram Samvat 1137 Vaishakh sudi 7. It does not mention the day. Along with the sun's transit it mentions the karana but does not give its name. By mathematical calculation based on Vikram Samvat the date comes to Monday, 30 March 1080 CE.

items.note: As per the epigraphic custom of the time, the author's name is recorded: Pandit Mahipal, son of Pandit Shringvas.
items.gloss: According to the inscription-writing tradition of the time, the writer of these lines is also recorded. It is the great work of Pandit Mahipal, son of Pandit Shringvas.

items.note: Inscriptions on both sides of the eastern entrance; one at the upper left corner names 'Shriman Udayadityanripati'.
items.gloss: You enter the temple touching countless inscriptions on both sides of the temple's eastern entrance. In the upper corner on the left you can clearly see the name 'Shriman Udayadityanripati' in one inscription.

items.note: Describes Santosh Kumar Verma's study of the inscriptions read so far, with translation, analysis and comparison with other Paramara inscriptions.
items.gloss: He has closely examined the inscriptions read so far. Not just translation but, with very good analysis, comparing them with other inscriptions of the Paramara period, he has made a relevant attempt to understand and explain a thousand-year-old era.

items.note: Quoting Verma: the date in this inscription is the first recorded date of Udayaditya's reign, which makes it most important.
items.gloss: The importance of this inscription is greatest because the date recorded in it is the first recorded date of Maharaja Udayaditya's reign.

claim.value: VS 1137 is the first recorded date of his reign (Verma)

items.note: Language and script of the six-line record: Sanskrit, 11th-century Nagari, prose-dominant with one verse in anushtubh metre.
items.gloss: This Sanskrit text is in the eleventh-century Nagari script. A prose-dominant style is used. One shloka is in anushtubh metre and the rest is in prose.

items.note: The inscription records Udayaditya performing the flag-hoisting at the Shri Udayeshvaradeva temple, and gives the temple's name as 'Udayeshvara Deva ka mandir'.
items.gloss: It says that on the said date Maharaja Udayaditya performed the auspicious flag-hoisting at the Shri Udayeshvaradeva temple. The present temple's name is written as 'Temple of Udayeshvara Deva'.

items.note: Opening verse of the record as given with translation: may King Udayaditya make the earth under one umbrella.
items.gloss: Hail. May King Udayaditya make the earth under a single umbrella.

items.note: Closing lines: the verse is by Pandit Shri Mahipala, son of Shringvasa; dated Samvat 1137 Vaisakha sudi 7.
items.gloss: This shloka is by Pandit Shri Shringvasa's son, Pandit Shri Mahipala. Samvat 1137 Vaisakha sudi 7.

items.note: Final line records completion of the flag-hoisting of Udayeshvara Deva, dated Samvat 1137 Vaisakha sudi 7.
items.gloss: Samvat 1137 Vaisakha sudi 7. The flag-hoisting of Shri Udayeshvara Deva is completed. May great fortune (Mahalakshmi) be auspicious.

items.note: Says this inscription has long been in ASI records.
items.gloss: It is not that no one knew about this inscription earlier. It has been in the ASI's records for quite some time.

items.note: Lists early published notices of the inscription: Cunningham (ASR vol. 10, p. 83, printed 1880), Bhandarkar (Progress Report ASI Western Circle 1913-14, p. 22), and M. B. Garde (Annual Report, Archaeological Dept, Gwalior State, Samvat 1974).
items.gloss: First Major General Alexander Cunningham mentioned it in Archaeological Survey of India Report, part 10, page 83. It was first printed in 1880. Historian D. R. Bhandarkar gave details of this inscription on page 22 of the Progress Report of the Archaeological Survey Western Circle 1913-14. Besides this, M. B. Garde mentions it in the Annual Report of the Archaeological Department in Gwalior State, Samvat 1974.
refs: Bhandarkar, Progress Report ASI Western Circle 1913-14, p. 22
Garde, Annual Report of the Archaeological Department, Gwalior State, Samvat 1974

items.note: Another inscription of the temple is dated VS 1116 and Saka 981, given as 1059 CE.
items.gloss: In another inscription of the Udaypur temple the date Vikram Samvat 1116 and Shaka Samvat 981 is engraved. By the English calendar this year is 1059 CE.

items.note: Limits of the evidence: a long 22-line record full of errors in language, grammar and craftsmanship, making meaningful translation difficult.
items.gloss: This is quite a long text. This inscription of 22 lines, full of errors, has incorrect language and grammar and also deficiencies in craftsmanship. These are reasons why meaningful translations are not easy.

items.note: This record begins with Shiva worship and turns to Udayaditya; its verses 2 and 3 give a genealogy of a Paramara king and his son Gandal as quoted by the author.
items.gloss: Like other Paramara inscriptions it begins with worship of Shiva and goes on to tell about Udayaditya. Each inscription gives some new information. It throws new light on the relation between Bhoja and Udayaditya, seen faintly in the haze of time. Its second verse says a heroic, learned Paramara king established the Malwa kingdom and punished sinners. From him a renowned son named Gandal (Gondal), devout, generous, discerning, who conquered all enemies, became famous for his glory.

items.note: Verses 3 and 5 as quoted: the father (Pata/Jnata) won a kingdom and built water-furnished temples; Udayaditya was deemed worthy and made king.
items.gloss: In the third verse: his son Pata (Jnata) crushed enemy armies, obtained the kingdom and gained fame like his forefathers; he built temples with reservoirs. The fifth verse says: giver of abundant gold and grain to Brahmins, he regarded Udayaditya as worthy, made him king and accumulated fame.

items.note: Verma's analysis: Udayaditya's father named as Pata/Jnata points to a junior Paramara branch, not Sindhuraja's line; possibly a feudatory of Bhoja ruling eastern Malwa including Vidisha, with Udaypur developing as an important centre.
items.gloss: Verma stops here to analyse. He says that the mention of 'Pata' or 'Jnata' as Udayaditya's father is a point suggesting new indications. One meaning is that Udayaditya did not descend from Sindhuraja's line but belonged to a junior branch of the Paramara dynasty. On this basis it can be assumed that Udayaditya probably ruled in the eastern part of Malwa as a chief feudatory under Maharaja Bhoja. Vidisha was also in this region. Then Udaypur must have begun to develop under it as an important centre.

claim.value: junior Paramara branch, not Sindhuraja's line; probable feudatory of Bhoja (Verma)

items.note: Possibility raised that after Jayasimha I was killed around 1070 CE by Chalukyas of Kalyani and Karnatas attacking Dhara, Udayaditya came to the throne in the political vacuum.
items.gloss: It may also be that when the combined armies of the Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Karnatas attacked the capital Dhara and killed Bhoja's son and successor Jayasimha I around 1070 CE, Udayaditya came to the throne in the sudden political vacuum. The question of Udayaditya's relation to Raja Bhoja is more important.

claim.value: possible accession after Jayasimha I's death c. 1070 (suggested, not stated)

items.note: Shorgarh inscription of Udayaditya, lines 5-6, calls him 'meditating on the feet of' Bhojadeva.
items.gloss: Another link is added by Udayaditya's Shorgarh inscription. Its fifth and sixth lines say: 'Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara Shri Bhojadeva-padanudhyata Paramabhattaraka Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara Shri Udayadityadeva: well.'

items.note: Argues 'padanudhyata' means 'meditating on the feet' (praise), not succession, so the Shorgarh claim of direct succession from Bhoja is weakened; Gupta-era usage is cited.
items.gloss: Earlier historians of the Gupta period believed that 'tatpadanudhyata' speaks directly of a successor. But in the Kakanadabota (Sanchi) and Udayagiri inscriptions, Atrakadavarda and Virasena Shaba are called tatpadanudhyata of Chandragupta II, who were trusted commanders. Hence the literal meaning 'meditating on the feet' was considered more apt; it is praise with no relation to succession. So the claim of direct succession from Bhoja to Udayaditya weakens here.

claim.value: padanudhyata = praise, not direct succession (as argued)

items.note: The Udaipur prashasti has the fullest account of the Paramara line up to Udayaditya and was prepared by Udayaditya himself.
items.gloss: The famous Udaypur prashasti has the most detailed account of the Paramara dynasty up to Udayaditya. This text was prepared by Udayaditya himself.

claim.value: most detailed account of Paramaras up to Udayaditya; commissioned by Udayaditya

items.note: Translation of Udaypur prashasti verse 21: after Bhoja's death the earth was covered in darkness of enemies and Udayaditya rose like the sun. (Sanskrit lines in this chunk are OCR-damaged.)
items.gloss: After the Shiva-devotee (Bhojadeva), whose glory was like the sun, went to heaven, when the whole earth like the city of Dhara was covered by the darkness of enemies and his traditional warriors had grown weak, then Udayadityadeva, like the sun, rose, destroying the towering darkness of enemies with the rays of his sword and gladdening all people.

items.note: Nagpur prashasti verse 32 of Naravarman, translated: Udayaditya, 'bandhu' of Bhoja, rescued the earth afflicted by Karna and other kings; the author notes the word 'bandhu' has several senses.
items.gloss: After he (Bhojadeva) attained the kinship of Indra and the lord of the kingdom's kinsmen were sunk in the water of conflict, his bandhu Udayaditya became king, who, like the Varaha incarnation, rescued the earth troubled by the Karnata Karna and others joined like an ocean. Here Udayaditya is called Bhojadeva's 'bandhu'. This is a noteworthy word. In dharmashastra there are three kinds of bandhu: atmabandhu, pitribandhu and matribandhu. Besides, relatives, brotherhood and family kin are also called bandhu.
